questions.q: Why does committing to a fixed status page update cadence (e.g. every 30 minutes) matter, even when there's no technical progress to report?
options: Silence between updates damages trust more than slow progress does — "still investigating, next update by X" is itself useful information
Status page tooling automatically deletes updates if too much time passes between them
Customers only read the very first update and ignore all later ones
It is a legal requirement in most jurisdictions for any public-facing service
questions.explain: A fixed cadence means an update goes out whether or not there's new technical information, so customers never experience silence as neglect.

questions.q: What are the two opposite mistakes in outage communication that both erode trust?
options: Updating too frequently, and updating in too much technical detail
Minimizing the actual impact (calling something intermittent when it's widespread), and over-promising a fix time before the root cause is confirmed
Using the word "investigating," and posting updates outside business hours
Posting to the internal stakeholder update before the public status page
questions.explain: Minimizing impact costs credibility the moment affected customers see through it, and an ETA that slips reads worse than giving no ETA at all.

questions.q: What is the standard four-stage status page lifecycle described in this lesson?
options: Detected, Escalated, Mitigated, Closed
Open, Paged, Fixed, Archived
Reported, Reviewed, Approved, Published
Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, Resolved
questions.explain: Investigating says "we know, we're on it"; Identified says the cause was found; Monitoring confirms the fix is holding; Resolved closes the loop and promises a fuller explanation.

questions.q: Why is the internal stakeholder update meant to be a different document from the public status page, rather than the same text trimmed down?
options: The public page is deliberately light on technical detail, while the internal update needs the real root cause, business impact, and enough detail for support and leadership to act on
They're meant to be identical; any difference is considered a communication failure
The public page needs more technical detail so customers can self-diagnose
Internal stakeholders don't need any business impact information, only engineers do
questions.explain: Writing one document and trimming it for two audiences tends to fail in one direction or the other — either leaking internal detail publicly, or leaving the internal update too vague to inform a real decision.

questions.q: Why is maintaining update cadence and consistent honesty during an outage typically owned by a dedicated Communications Lead rather than whoever is debugging the issue?
options: Because customers prefer not to hear from engineers directly, as a matter of brand policy
Because the Communications Lead role is purely ceremonial and has no real content to produce
Because someone actively debugging a shifting technical picture can't also reliably hold a fixed update schedule and a consistent honesty level at the same time
Because only non-technical staff are legally permitted to post to a public status page
questions.explain: This is the direct payoff of separating roles: because the Communications Lead isn't also debugging the problem, they can maintain cadence and honesty even as the technical picture keeps changing underneath them.
